chapters.covers: Fitting goggles so they seal, choosing chest-deep water where your feet always reach the floor, and putting your face in calmly with a lifeguard on duty.
chapters.hook: Most nerves in the pool come down to two fixable things: leaky goggles and deep water.
chapters.outcome: You can stand in chest-deep water with sealed goggles, put your face in, and look at the floor for 5 seconds without flinching.
chapters.title: Goggles on, feet down, face in

chapters.covers: Humming out a steady stream of air through your nose or mouth underwater, then bobbing up for a quick breath in, over and over.
chapters.hook: Holding your breath feels safer underwater, yet it's the habit that tires beginners out first.
chapters.outcome: You can do 10 bobs in a row: breathe out slowly underwater, pop up, take a quick breath in, and go back down.
chapters.title: Breathe out under, breathe in above

chapters.covers: Looking straight down so your hips rise, pushing off into a streamlined glide with arms forward and ears between your upper arms, and standing up safely by tucking your knees first.
chapters.hook: Your hips sink because of where your eyes point. Move your gaze and your legs come up.
chapters.outcome: You can push off the wall, glide flat for 3 to 5 metres with your face down, then tuck your knees and stand up without a splash.
chapters.title: Lie flat and glide

chapters.covers: A flutter kick that starts at the hips with long legs, pointed toes and loose ankles, practised holding a kickboard.
chapters.hook: Bending your knees harder can make you go slower. The power comes from somewhere higher up.
chapters.outcome: You can kick across the shallow end holding a kickboard, legs nearly straight and toes pointed, moving forward steadily.
chapters.title: The motor: kicking from the hips

chapters.covers: Hand going in fingertips first in line with your shoulder, pulling water back toward your hip, then lifting the arm out with a high elbow to start again.
chapters.hook: Your hand isn't pushing you down the pool. It's holding on to water while your body moves past it.
chapters.outcome: You can glide, kick and take 6 to 8 alternating arm strokes, each pulling back to your hip, with your face still down.
chapters.title: The oars: one arm stroke done right

chapters.covers: Rolling your whole body onto its side to breathe instead of lifting your head, keeping one goggle lens underwater, and breathing in quickly while your front arm stays reaching forward.
chapters.hook: Lifting your head to breathe is exactly what makes your legs sink. There's a lower, easier way.
chapters.outcome: You can swim 10 metres of front crawl taking side breaths, without lifting your head or stopping to stand.
chapters.title: The porthole: breathing to the side

chapters.covers: Choosing a slow, steady stroke you could keep up for a long time, swimming 10 to 15 metre stretches to build trust, then putting together the full length.
chapters.hook: Swimming slower is often what gets beginners across the pool. Here's why speed runs out first.
chapters.outcome: You can swim one full length of the pool in front crawl, breathing to the side, without stopping.
chapters.title: Fuel for one length

plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14, not promised: two lengths back to back with a short rest at the wall between them.
plan.horizon28: Further out, around day 28, not promised: 4 to 6 lengths in one session, with some breaths taken to your other side.
plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to swim one full length of a pool (often 25 metres) in front crawl, breathing to the side, without stopping or grabbing the wall.

picture.name: Your body as a boat

verdict.best: The chapters build one skill at a time toward the full length. Each has a measurable outcome and a hook that corrects a common beginner myth.

clarity.why: The wording is plain, short and concrete, with no filler.

coverage.why: All seven outline parts are covered in order, and nothing off-goal is added. The extras are limited to the horizon and next lines.

fidelity.why: The plan follows the brief's facts. The specific numbers (5 seconds, 10 bobs, 6 to 8 strokes, the 14- and 28-day horizons) are not in the brief, though they are reasonable and the horizons are marked as not promised. The lifeguard mention is a small addition.

framing.why: This is a course, so there is no framing line.

goalFit.why: Every chapter builds toward one unbroken length for a new adult swimmer, and the plan is well pitched to a beginner.

hooks.why: Most are concrete and surprising, such as the hips sinking because of where your eyes point and swimming slower to get across. Chapter 1's hook is flatter and more generic.

outcomes.why: They are specific and measurable, such as 10 bobs, a 3 to 5 m glide and 10 m of side breathing. A few numbers are invented, and a 10 m breathing swim in chapter 6 is a big jump from chapter 5.

picture.why: The boat maps the hull, motor, oars, porthole and fuel, and it carries through the chapter titles. The hull and fuel parts are a little loose, and the boat is a fairly common comparison.

progression.why: The order runs from comfort to breathing, floating, kick, arms, side breathing, then pacing. Each chapter teaches one thing.

chapters.covers: Picking goggles that seal, and getting easy in chest-deep water where your feet always reach the floor.

chapters.covers: Humming out a steady stream of bubbles through your nose or mouth, then bobbing up for a quick breath in.
chapters.hook: The fix for gasping isn't holding your breath longer. It's doing the opposite.
chapters.outcome: You can do 10 bobs in a row: breathe out slowly underwater, then pop up and breathe in fast.
chapters.title: Breathe out underwater

chapters.covers: Looking straight down to lift your hips, pushing off into a front glide with ears between your arms, and tucking your knees to stand up safely.
chapters.hook: Where you point your eyes decides whether your legs sink or float.
chapters.outcome: You can push off the wall, glide flat for a few metres with your face down, and stand up again without a scramble.
chapters.title: Float flat and glide

chapters.covers: The flutter kick: long legs moving from the hips, toes pointed, ankles loose, practised with a kickboard.
chapters.hook: Kicking harder from the knees can actually slow you down. Here's where the kick really starts.
chapters.outcome: You can kick across the shallow end holding a kickboard, legs near the surface, without bending hard at the knees.
chapters.title: Kick from the hips

chapters.covers: The freestyle arm stroke: fingertips enter in line with your shoulder, pull water back to your hip, lift the elbow high to bring the arm forward.
chapters.hook: Your hand isn't sweeping water aside. It's pushing it back past your hip. That changes everything.
chapters.outcome: You can glide and add arm strokes over 10 metres, with your breath held and your hands pushing water back toward your hips.
chapters.title: Pull with your arms

chapters.covers: Rolling your whole body along its length to take a fast mouth breath while one arm reaches forward, keeping one goggle lens underwater.
chapters.hook: How do you breathe without lifting your head? Keep one goggle in the water.
chapters.outcome: You can swim 10 to 15 metres of freestyle, taking side breaths without lifting your head or stopping.
chapters.title: Breathe to the side

chapters.covers: Choosing a slow, steady stroke rate, building up from 10 to 15 metre pieces, then going for the full length.
chapters.hook: On your first full length, slower strokes get you further than faster ones. Here's why.
chapters.outcome: You can pace yourself and swim one full length of the pool without stopping.
chapters.title: Swim the whole length

plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14, you might link two lengths with only a short rest at the wall.
plan.horizon28: Later, around day 28, you might swim four lengths in a row, or start breathing to both sides.
plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to push off the wall and swim one full length of freestyle (usually 25 metres) without stopping, breathing to the side as you go.

chapters.covers: Before 1914, Europe split into two rival alliances: the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy (formed 1882) and the Triple Entente of Britain, France and Russia (1907). Competition for colonies and a naval arms race raised tension, and nationalist movements in the Balkans destabilised Austria-Hungary from inside.
chapters.hook: Before 1914, Europe was split into two armed camps. One quarrel could become everyone's war.
chapters.outcome: You can name both alliances and their members, and explain why a local quarrel in the Balkans could pull in every major power.
chapters.title: Europe splits into two armed camps

chapters.covers: The chain of events from Archduke Franz Ferdinand's assassination by a Serbian nationalist on 28 June 1914. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July. Russia mobilised to defend Serbia. Germany declared war on Russia and France in August. Britain joined after Germany invaded neutral Belgium.
chapters.hook: How did one murder in Sarajevo pull five great powers into war in about five weeks?
chapters.outcome: You can retell the five steps from the assassination to Britain entering the war, in order, and explain why each country acted.
chapters.title: From Sarajevo to world war

chapters.covers: The Russian, German, Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires collapsed. Russia fell to the Bolshevik Revolution in 1917, and Austria-Hungary broke into new states such as Austria, Hungary and Czechoslovakia. The 1919 Treaty of Versailles imposed reparations (war payments) and land losses on Germany. Former Ottoman lands became British and French mandates, territories the two powers ran on the League's behalf. The peace treaties created the League of Nations. The war killed an estimated 15 to 22 million people, and its grievances and economic damage set the stage for World War II.
chapters.hook: Four empires vanished in this war, and the borders drawn afterwards still shape today's headlines.
chapters.outcome: You can name the four fallen empires, say what Versailles demanded of Germany, and explain two ways the settlement led toward World War II.
chapters.title: Four empires fall, a new map is drawn

plan.framing: This doesn't need weeks. Three short chapters will take you from why it started to how it changed the map.
next: How Middle East borders were drawn
plan.outcome7: By the end you'll be able to explain step by step how one assassination in Sarajevo in 1914 became a world war, name the four empires the war destroyed, and say how the 1919 peace helped set up World War II.

verdict.best: Chapters 1 and 2 give a clean causal path from alliances to the assassination to the war's outbreak. The outcomes are testable and the sources are real.

clarity.why: Plain and concrete, with 'reparations' explained. The chapter 3 'covers' text is dense.

coverage.why: All six outline items are folded into three chapters. Nothing extra is added. The war's course and its human cost get very little space.

fidelity.why: The facts match the brief. 'Five great powers in about five weeks' and 'five steps' are small inferences. The mandates 'on the League's behalf' gloss is outside the brief, though true. Today's headlines is an unsupported claim.

framing.why: It is natural and fits the topic, running from why it started to how it changed the map. The opening sentence is a little generic.

goalFit.why: It serves a new reader who wants to know why the war started and how it changed the world. Chapter 3 is overloaded, and the 'changed the world' half gets only one chapter.

hooks.why: Chapter 2's hook is a good specific question. Chapter 1's hook only restates the title and is flat. Chapter 3's hook is vague, and the claim about borders in today's headlines is not in the brief.

verdict.why: Plan A has more specific, measurable outcomes (5 seconds, 10 bobs, 3 to 5 metres, 10 metres side-breathing) and a boat picture that carries through every chapter, including the porthole and the fuel. Plan B is sound but vaguer, with outcomes like "several strokes" and "part of the pool", and fewer sources. I would give the writer Plan A.

Plan B has more specific, measurable outcomes (3 to 5 m glide, 6 to 8 strokes, 10 m of side breathing) and a boat picture that carries through the chapters (motor, oars, porthole, fuel). It also adds the safety details of feet reaching the floor and a lifeguard on duty, and it is more honest about the later horizons. Plan A is solid but vaguer, and its picture stops after the arms and kick.

Plan A's outcomes build measurably toward the full length (10 bobs, 10 m, 10-15 m, then the full length), and its boat picture and three sources fit the goal well. Plan B is slightly more faithful to the brief, but its ch5 and ch6 outcomes stay below the goal and its picture and sources are thinner.

Plan A's outcomes are more honest and reachable, and its rowing picture carries through consistently. Plan B has stronger hooks and sources, but its chapter 5 outcome ('breath held') and chapter 6 outcome (swimming 10 to 15 m with side breaths) jump ahead in the progression, and its day-28 'four lengths' goes beyond the brief.

Plan A gives the writer the specific brief facts in each chapter (dates, members, the reparations and mandates explained in plain terms) and sets more concrete, checkable outcomes. Plan B has a slightly cleaner split, with the Balkans placed alongside the assassination, but its chapter 3 is overloaded and its covers are vaguer.

Plan B covers every brief fact, including Versailles reparations, the Bolshevik Revolution, and a plain-language gloss for mandates. Its outcomes are concrete and reachable. Plan A has a tidier chapter 1 and a more accurate hook, but it leaves out Versailles' demands on Germany and the Balkan setup.

Plan A is more specific and accurate. Its chapter 3 outcome names the four empires and links the peace terms to WWII, and its covers include the death toll. Plan B's outcome7 promises 'four ways the war still shapes today's map', which chapter 3 never defines, and its hook says 'five great powers were at war within weeks', which is looser than A's wording.

Plan B covers the Balkan nationalism trigger, the casualty figure and the full set of chapter outcomes that the brief requires, and its outcome7 names the four empires and the link to WWII. Plan A leaves out the Balkan crisis and the death toll, and its outcome7 promises "four ways the war still shapes today's map", which chapter 3 does not clearly deliver.
